Empirical Research Plan:  Inter-industry Trade Links and the Propagation of Mergers (1986-2010)

------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------
Strategy Instrumental‐Variables (shift-share / “Bartik” IV) implemented in a two-stage panel model with industry and year fixed effects.

Intuition We want the causal effect of merger activity in an industry’s trading partners on the industry’s own probability of merging.  
• Endogenous regressor: weighted sum of realised mergers in directly connected supplier and customer industries.  
• Instrument: the same IO weights interacted with exogenous, industry-specific merger *shifters* that are orthogonal to the focal industry’s unobservables.

Why IV is appropriate  
(a) Merger counts in trading partners are likely correlated with omitted shocks that also affect the focal industry (e.g., macro cycles, technology).  
(b) Pre-determined IO coefficients (1982–2002 tables) supply the *shares*; shifters such as Harford-style Q-dispersion shocks, large regulatory events (e.g., 1990 Spotted Owl), or industry-level demand/price shocks are plausibly exogenous.  
(c) The Bartik design exploits cross-sectional heterogeneity in initial trade exposure and time-series heterogeneity in shocks, delivering quasi-random variation in predicted neighbour mergers.

------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------
Endogenous “treatment” variable 
 Exposure_it ≡ Σ_j w_ij · Mergers_jt  
 w_ij = industry-i purchases from j as share of i’s total inputs (or sales shares for downstream exposure) taken from the *closest* pre-sample IO table (1982 for 1986–91, 1987 for 1992–96, etc.).  

Instrument (first stage) 
 PredictedExposure_it ≡ Σ_j w_ij · Shock_jt  
 Shock_jt is an exogenous merger shifter for industry j in year t:  
  (1) Harford (2005) style “asset revaluation” shock (|Δ industry-median Q|), or  
  (2) Binary indicators for large, plausibly exogenous regulatory/technological events (e.g., Spotted Owl listing, 1996 Telecom Act), or  
  (3) Leave-one-out national merger wave intensity (industry-j’s share of national mergers lagged).  

Control group / counterfactual Industries with low IO-based exposure to the shocked industries act as controls in each year; fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences.

Timing Annual panel, 1986–2010.  Lag the endogenous variable one year to avoid mechanical simultaneity (i   merges this year cannot causally depend on j merging this same year).

------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------
A1 Relevance Trade-weighted shocks are strongly correlated with realised neighbour mergers.  Plausible: shocks trigger mergers in the directly hit industry, and IO weights pick up substantial variation (to be verified in the 1st stage).

A2 Exclusion PredictedExposure affects focal-industry mergers only through its effect on *neighbour* mergers, not via any direct channel once we control for focal-industry shocks and year FE.  Plausible because the shifters are *industry-specific* and the weights are technological parameters unrelated to focal-industry fundamentals.

A3 Predetermined Shares IO coefficients are measured before the shock and change slowly; thus they are exogenous to post-1986 merger decisions.

A4 Parallel Trends of Unobservables Any time-varying shocks common to industries with similar IO structure are captured by year FE or observable controls (industry Q, R&D, volatility, etc.).

A5 Stable Exposure No general-equilibrium feedback from the focal industry to the instrument within the same year (reasonable given lagging).

------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------
T1 Correlated Shocks across Network  
 • Approach: include *own* industry shock_jt in the control set; double-cluster SEs by (industry, year).  
 • Leave-one-out construction of Shock_jt at the national level removes focal-industry influence.

T2 Measurement Error in IO Weights or NAICS–IO Mapping  
 • Sensitivity checks with alternative weights (Use table vs. Make table, 124-industry vs. 471-industry aggregation).  
 • Re-estimate dropping hub industries whose IO links are especially noisy (wholesale, retail).

T3 Violation of Exclusion via Direct Demand Channel  
 • Downstream exposure modelled separately from upstream; include contemporaneous demand controls (industry sales growth, price indices).  
 • Placebo test: use *future* shocks (t+2) as instrument; coefficient should be zero.

------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)         # fast FE and IV
library(multiwayvcov)   # clustering
library(lmtest)

# -------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# -------------------------------------------
merg <- fread("SDC_mergers_industry_year.csv")        # vars: iocode, year, n_mergers
io   <- fread("IO_weights_471.csv")                  # vars: buyer_i, seller_j, w_ij
shock<- fread("industry_shocks.csv")                 # vars: iocode, year, shock_value
controls <- fread("industry_controls.csv")           # vars: iocode, year, q, rdcapex, mb, ...

# -------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct exposure measures
# -------------------------------------------
# Neighbor merger counts
merg_jt   <- merg[, .(seller_j = iocode, year, n_mergers_j = n_mergers)]

# Weight * realized mergers
exp_dt <- merge(io, merg_jt, by = "seller_j", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
exp_dt[, exposure := w_ij * n_mergers_j]

# Sum over j for each buyer-industry-year
exp_it <- exp_dt[, .(Exposure = sum(exposure, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(buyer_i, year)]

# Instrument: Weight * exogenous shock
shk_dt <- merge(io, shock, by.x = "seller_j", by.y = "iocode", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
shk_dt[, pred := w_ij * shock_value]
bartik <- shk_dt[, .(PredExposure = sum(pred, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(buyer_i, year)]

# -------------------------------------------
# 3. Merge everything
# -------------------------------------------
Y <- merg[, .(buyer_i = iocode, year, mergers_i = n_mergers)]
panel <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by = c("buyer_i","year"), all = TRUE),
                list(Y, exp_it, bartik, controls))

panel[is.na(panel)] <- 0             # keep zeros explicit

# -------------------------------------------
# 4. Main specification: 2SLS with industry & year FE
# -------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- mergers_i ~ q + rdcapex + mb | q + rdcapex + mb + PredExposure

est <- feols(iv_formula, data = panel,
             fixef = ~ buyer_i + year, cluster = ~ buyer_i + year)

summary(est)

# -------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: alternative IO aggregation
# -------------------------------------------
# Repeat with 124-industry weights
io124 <- fread("IO_weights_124.csv")
# ...recompute Exposure and PredExposure, re-estimate est_alt

# -------------------------------------------
# 6. Placebo test: future shocks as instrument
panel[, PredExp_lead2 := shift(PredExposure, 2, type = "lead"), by = buyer_i]
est_placebo <- feols(mergers_i ~ q + rdcapex | q + rdcapex + PredExp_lead2,
                     data = panel, fixef = ~ buyer_i + year,
                     cluster = ~ buyer_i + year)
summary(est_placebo)
```

------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------
Theory suggests positive propagation: when suppliers or customers consolidate, impacted firms respond defensively (secure inputs, bargaining position) or offensively (vertical integration).  I expect:

Elasticity ≈ 0.10–0.15 One additional merger among trading partners (weighted by their IO share equal to a one-standard-deviation change) raises the focal industry’s own merger probability by roughly 10–15 percent off a baseline of ~3–4 percent per year.

Effects should be stronger:  
• Downstream (customer) than upstream, because output market power passes upstream.  
• For industries with high concentration or asset specificity.

------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
------------------------------------------------------
C1 Instrument relevance……………………………………1  
C2 Exclusion restriction……………………………………0.5 (possible direct demand channel)  
C3 Predetermined shares…………………………………1  
C4 No weak instruments (F-stat > 10)………………1 (to be checked)  
C5 SUTVA / no interference outside IO links…0.5 (second-round network effects possible)  

Total = 4/5 → Reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.
